rationale: The definitions agree: additive category, all kernels and cokernels, and every canonical coimage-to-image map is an isomorphism.
Grothendieck's additive category is the Stacks preadditive category with zero object and binary biproducts; Stacks packages this as finite products.

The core categorical data and axioms agree, but neither convention contains the other literally: the source requires a nonempty, possibly proper class of objects and pairwise disjoint Hom sets, while Stacks uses a set of objects, permits the empty category, and does not impose global disjointness. This is a convention-sensitive extension, not an equivalence.
No labelled local definition matches the dual generator notion, and the source's AB5-plus-generator existence assertion is only mentioned without proof in the local tree.
Stacks defines diagrams as functors from an index category, not Grothendieck's category of representations of a bare graph scheme with imposed relations; no labelled exact target was found.
No labelled local target defines Grothendieck's triple of vertex set, arrow set, and direction map independently of composition.
The object map, morphism maps, identity preservation, and composition preservation agree exactly for covariant functors.
The factorization-through-proper-subobjects criterion agrees, but the source defines it for a category with subobjects whereas Stacks states it inside an abelian category.
The source inductive system is the Stacks system over a preorder and its inductive limit is precisely the colimit universal property.
Both define an arbitrary set-indexed product by the same universal property and canonical projections.
The source's arbitrary direct sum in a category is the Stacks coproduct, with the same universal property and canonical injections/coprojections.
Stacks gives the extension definition and proves its equivalence with exactness of Hom(-,I), exactly the two source formulations.
The source uses this as a heading for simultaneous inheritance of AB conditions by graph-relation diagram categories; no labelled local term or general theorem matches it.
The source projective system is the inverse system over a preorder and its projective limit is the Stacks limit universal property.
Stacks gives the lifting definition and its equivalent exactness-of-Hom characterization, matching the dual source notion.
Stacks constructs the same abelian Serre quotient and adds its universal property; Grothendieck's 'thick' subcategory is Stacks' Serre subcategory.
No labelled local definition encodes formal integral linear combinations of paths and auxiliary identity symbols as relations on diagrams.
No labelled local target defines R-commutative diagrams or the resulting additive graph-relation category C^Sigma.
Postcomposition by a functor is standard, but the local tree has no labelled statement matching the canonical extension F^Sigma, its functoriality in F, and preservation of exactness.
No labelled local definition covers families of cogenerators, and no labelled theorem states the source's AB5-plus-generator implication or module examples.
Stacks diagrams are functors and therefore already respect index-category composition; it does not label the source's separate graph path and loop relations.
The local tree uses commutative diagrams throughout but has no labelled general definition equating all parallel composite paths in a bare diagram scheme.

Grothendieck's special 'full subcategory' is exactly Stacks' weak Serre subcategory: ordinary fullness plus kernels, cokernels, and extensions; it is not merely a full subcategory in current terminology.
No labelled local target defines paths as nonempty finite arrow sequences in a bare graph; Stacks starts from an index category whose composites already exist.
A Stacks diagram is a functor from a category, while this unit builds a category of representations of a graph before imposing path relations; no exact labelled target exists.
Opposite categories are defined locally, but no labelled target defines reversal of a bare graph scheme together with retained additive relations.
The compatibility and universal mapping clauses are exactly the colimit of the associated preorder-indexed diagram.
Stacks gives functoriality for a transformation together with a change of index category; the fixed-index colimit functor asserted here is the special case H=id.
The induced map between colimits is exactly the H=id case of the more general local functorial-colimit lemma.
Stacks defines injective targets by the lifting property. Every monomorphism into such a target is a source effacement, but an effacement A→M need not make M injective (for example A=0).
The extension property is the Stacks definition and exactness of Hom(-,M) is its labelled equivalent characterization.

Quasi-equality means that the inclusion or quotient map has kernel and cokernel in the Serre subcategory and hence becomes invertible in the Stacks localization; Stacks does not name this relation separately.
The resulting abelian quotient and exact essentially-surjective functor agree; Stacks constructs it as a localization and additionally proves the universal property.
Both constructions compose representatives in the Serre localization, but Stacks uses fraction calculus rather than the source's simultaneous subobject-to-quotient representative Q.
This completes the source's representative-level composition and abelian-category verification; Stacks proves those facts through multiplicative-system localization, not this explicit Q construction.

Stacks gives each one-sided filtered-colimit formula for morphisms in a localization; the source uses a simultaneous double system of quasi-equal subobjects and quotients, which is not stated verbatim.
The source's two-sided representatives model the same Serre localization; Stacks labels left and right fractions separately and does not state this exact simultaneous equivalence relation.
Objects and arrows are subsets, identities and composition are inherited, and the inclusion is a functor in both definitions.
The source additionally requires each Hom subset to be a subgroup for an additive subcategory; the two local definitions supply the ingredients but do not label this combined notion.
Grothendieck's 'thick' condition is exactly Stacks' Serre subcategory condition and its closure under zero, isomorphism, subquotients, and extensions.
The square is the naturality condition defining a morphism of source graph-valued diagrams; it has no independently labelled local target apart from the unmatched parent construction.

The diagram illustrates the effacement lifting square. The local injective-object definition supplies the corresponding lift only when the target is injective, so the diagram is not an independent theorem.
No labelled local result identifies, for an arbitrary additive category, the subcategory of objects annihilated by an integer as a graph-relation diagram category with inherited AB properties.
Stacks labels the binary product category, while the source uses an arbitrary set-indexed product C^I and its graph-scheme presentation.
The claim about arbitrary products of integer-annihilator subcategories as relation-diagram categories has no exact labelled local counterpart.
The local tree uses arrow categories informally but has no labelled definition matching the source graph presentation and its optional integer-annihilation relations.

Stacks gives the same functors and natural transformations and notes their category, but does not identify it with Grothendieck's graph-with-relations category or add the additive-functor relation presentation.

Stacks develops the same category of complexes and proves it abelian when the value category is abelian; the source additionally presents complexes, bounded variants, and bicomplexes as graph relations.
No labelled local target treats G-objects in an arbitrary category as a one-vertex diagram scheme with group-law relations and inherits the full permanence theorem.
No labelled local target defines objects of an arbitrary additive category with a unital ring action and identifies them with this relation-diagram construction.
The objects, transition maps, identity maps, and composition law are exactly Stacks' system over a preordered set; only the graph-relation presentation differs.
Stacks identifies systems and inverse systems over a preorder and defines a presheaf as the corresponding contravariant functor; this matches the source examples.
The footnote correctly checks that ordered-index inductive systems satisfy the printed syntactic hypotheses, but those hypotheses do not rescue the false generator conclusion of Proposition 1.9.2.
Both state the generator-subobject lifting criterion for injectivity in an AB5/Grothendieck abelian category.
The local proof uses the same Zorn maximal-extension argument, generator map, pullback subobject, and AB5 union step, with modernized notation.

Stacks proves pointwise additive/abelian permanence for inverse systems and complexes, but has no labelled theorem for arbitrary additive graph relations, products/sums, or every AB1-AB6 and dual axiom.
The componentwise kernel/cokernel proof is reflected only in these labelled special cases; Stacks does not reproduce the general relation-diagram proof or all AB permanence claims.
Stacks covers AB3 existence of colimits, their general right exactness, and AB5 exactness, but the labelled targets do not state the source's explicit kernel-supremum formula.
Both construct colimits from coproducts and coequalizer-type relations; the source specializes this to quotients in an abelian category.
This completes the quotient construction; the remaining exactness and kernel assertions are left unproved in the source and are only partly covered by the Stacks AB discussion.

Stacks defines a singleton generator and proves the quotient-of-a-sum consequence under the stronger Grothendieck hypotheses; it does not label the source's full family/sum/generator equivalence under AB3 alone.
The evaluation-map quotient argument appears locally, but only as one implication under Grothendieck-category hypotheses; the source's other equivalences are not separately labelled.

Direct authority review confirms that the last assertion is false. For the one-arrow scheme 1 to 2 in Ab, D=(Z identity-to Z) has the proper subdiagram B=(2Z to Z), but every map from the proposed epsilon-family factors through B. The valid first membership assertion remains source history; no Stacks theorem is claimed for the false generator assertion.

The embedded proof is invalid because Hom(epsilon_s(A),D)=Hom(A,D(s)) fails when s has outgoing arrows. It inherits the authority-confirmed source-error disposition of Proposition 1.9.2 and supplies no independent Stacks target.
Stacks proves the quotient is abelian, the quotient functor exact and essentially surjective with kernel the Serre subcategory, and adds the universal property.

The local tree has functorial spectral-sequence results in specific constructions but no labelled general statement that applying a Serre quotient kills selected terms and yields the asserted exact sequences modulo the subcategory.
Container for the source's basic category definitions; candidate mappings and boundaries are recorded on its descendant units.
Container for injective/projective definitions and the Grothendieck enough-injectives theorem; descendants carry the exact claim mappings.
Container for weak Serre/Serre subcategories and the Serre quotient; source terminology 'full/thick' differs from current Stacks terminology.

Composition, identities, and the Hom-set axioms agree, but neither convention contains the other literally: the source requires a nonempty, possibly proper class of objects and pairwise disjoint Hom sets, whereas Stacks uses a set of objects and permits the empty category. The comparison is therefore an explicit convention boundary.
Same objects, reversed morphisms, and reversed composition agree exactly; source writes dual category C^o where Stacks writes C^opp.
The mono/epi cancellation definitions agree. The source additionally calls them injective/surjective and calls a morphism satisfying both 'bijective', terminology Stacks reserves differently.
The two-sided inverse and isomorphism clauses agree, but the source also defines left/right inverses and records split mono/epi implications without a single matching local label.
The elementary closure and cancellation sorites for mono-, epi-, bijective, and isomorphisms are consequences of local definitions but are not stated under an exact labelled target.
Stacks does not give a labelled general-category construction of subobjects as equivalence classes of monomorphisms with the source's chosen representatives and induced order.
The dual ordered class of quotient objects in an arbitrary category has no exact labelled local definition; Stacks introduces quotients only in the abelian setting.

The arbitrary product universal property and canonical projections agree; the source also states functorial product maps and that products preserve monomorphisms, not all of which are in the labelled definition.
The arbitrary coproduct universal property agrees; the source additionally discusses sum morphisms and preservation of epimorphisms, beyond the labelled definition.
Container for functors, natural transformations, and equivalences; exact mappings are given on the three descendant units.
Covariant functors agree exactly, and both define contravariant functors through the opposite category; the source's multifunctor aside is not separately labelled.
The component maps, naturality square, identity, and vertical composition agree; both obtain a functor category when size permits.

The notions are mathematically equivalent, but the source chooses quasi-inverse data satisfying triangle identities whereas the Stacks definition only asks for inverse-up-to-isomorphism and separately characterizes fully faithful plus essentially surjective.
Container for Grothendieck's older additive-category package; Stacks separates the Hom-group condition as preadditive from the finite-biproduct/zero condition as additive.
The image, coimage, and canonical factorization Coim(u)→Im(u) agree with the labelled local definition and lemma.
Stacks uses kernel-of-cokernel as its definition of image. The source's smallest-subobject alternative and its equivalence only in abelian categories are not stated under a local label.
Stacks proves product iff coproduct for pairs in a preadditive category, defines the resulting biproduct, and gives the same zero-object characterizations.
The first part of the local lemma states exactly that the opposite of a preadditive/additive category is again preadditive/additive.
Kernels, cokernels, images, coimages, and the canonical factorization agree; the source's zero-divisor characterization of mono/epi is not separately stated in the labelled local targets.
Stacks uses the same Hom-group definition of additive functor and proves that such functors preserve zero objects and finite direct sums.
Container for AB1/AB2 and elementary abelian-category exactness; descendant units carry claim-level mappings.
The local definition includes exactly the existence of all kernels and cokernels; it bundles this source axiom with AB2.
The local definition includes exactly that every canonical Coim(f)→Im(f) is an isomorphism; it bundles this source axiom with AB1.
Stacks' left/right/exact functors and the short-exact-sequence criteria agree. The historical 'half-exact' condition at the middle term is not defined under these labels.
Exactness as image equals kernel, the short exact sequence, and both Hom criteria agree; source 'generalized cokernel' is current cokernel universal-property terminology.

Stacks proves mono plus epi iff isomorphism in an abelian category and gives the filtered-vector-space nonabelian example; the source lists additional topological and analytic examples absent from these targets.
This is a broad methodological assertion that all finite-character abelian-group diagram formalism transfers to any abelian category; no single labelled local theorem has that scope.
The subobject/quotient order anti-isomorphism and lattice formulas are not stated under an exact local label, although they follow from abelian-category infrastructure.
The source's systematic direct and inverse images for both subobjects and quotient objects have no exact labelled local definition or theorem.
Container for AB3-AB6 and their duals; Stacks labels AB3-AB5 and duals through AB5*, but has no AB6 entry.
Both define AB3 as existence of arbitrary direct sums in an abelian category.
Source AB4 asks sums of monomorphisms to be monic; Stacks says direct sums are exact. Under AB3 coproducts are already right exact, so these formulations agree.

Source gives the directed-subobject distributivity form; Stacks defines AB5 as exactness of filtered colimits. These are the standard equivalent formulations in an AB3 abelian category, though the equivalence is not proved at this label.
The extension of compatible maps from a directed union is the source's second AB5 formulation. Stacks states filtered-colimit exactness but does not label this exact Hom-extension reformulation.
The local Grothendieck-conditions definition stops at AB5/AB5* and contains no labelled arbitrary-intersection distributivity axiom AB6.
The local discussion records that AB3 gives all colimits and that direct sums/colimits are right exact before AB4/AB5; the source also writes the supremum-of-subobjects construction explicitly.
No single labelled local result reproduces the combined dual-axiom examples, independence statements, Pontryagin-duality example, sheaf-product failure, and AB5-plus-AB5* triviality claim.
Transition from AB axioms to limits and injective/projective objects; it contains no independent mathematical claim needing a target.
Container for Grothendieck's bare graph schemes, additive relations, and permanence theorem; Stacks has only special-case diagram categories, not this labelled general formalism.
Container for examples of the unmatched graph-with-relations formalism; descendant units record exact special-case overlaps where present.
Container for systems over preorders and their inductive/projective limits; proposition-level AB exactness boundaries are recorded below.
The generator criterion and deduction that subobjects form a set agree, but Stacks works in an abelian category and gives cardinal bounds; the source also defines families of generators.
The module and topological-space sheaf generator examples are standard, but no exact labelled local unit states this combined family in the source's extension-by-zero notation.
The local proof performs the same functorial first-stage attachment using all maps from subobjects of a generator; its pushout is the source cokernel construction in abelian notation.
Both iterate the first-stage functor by transfinite recursion and take colimits at limit ordinals.

Both stop at a sufficiently large-cofinality ordinal and use the generator-subobject criterion. Stacks explicitly chooses cofinality greater than |U|; the source chooses the least ordinal of larger cardinality and argues via its subobject cardinal.
Both prove that AB5 plus a generator gives enough injectives; the Stacks theorem states the stronger functorial embedding conclusion already at theorem level.
The source's functor M and natural monomorphism A→M(A) with injective targets are exactly Stacks' functorial injective embeddings.
No labelled local theorem gives injective effacements from AB3, AB4, AB3*, and a cogenerator; Stacks does not define this effacement notion.
No labelled local target states that a G-object injective in the operator category is injective after forgetting the action, under the source's functorial construction.

The remark's claimed stability of the generator hypothesis for the cited diagram categories depends on the false last assertion of Proposition 1.9.2. It is retained as a dependency-qualified historical statement, with no valid Stacks coverage asserted.
Stacks supplies the dual projective definition and characterizations, but not a labelled dual of the whole source theorem or a projective-effacement notion under dual AB hypotheses.
